_meta.description: Optional. Per-legislator AI summaries generated OFFLINE by Muse Spark from that legislator's statements. Each sentence must cite >= 1 statement_id from stances.json; the UI renders the citations as clickable numbers. Regenerate whenever stances change. Never generate at page load.
_meta.prompt_contract: Input: all statements for one legislator (quote, issue, date, score). Output: 2-4 neutral sentences describing their stance pattern, consistency over time, and where they diverge from their party; no adjectives of praise or blame; every sentence cites statement_ids it relies on.

sentences.text: On gun policy, Finch moved from opposing the background-check bill in 2025 to voting for it in 2026, tying the change to the rural-seller amendment and events in Sacramento.
He frames energy and infrastructure through district jobs and grid reliability: supportive of data-center buildout, skeptical of renewable subsidies.
On defense he backs the cyber budget increase without qualification.
Beaumont's positions are consistent across the record: opposed to new gun regulation, policing restrictions, AI licensing and corporate-tax increases, with no recorded shifts.
His gun-policy statements are the most repeated item in his record and are among the shortest, suggesting a settled position rather than an evolving one.
Marquez supports gun regulation, policing reform and Ukraine aid, and opposes the border bill, consistently pairing funding with accountability language.
Her policing position is repeated across sessions with the same framing, indicating a stable priority rather than a one-off vote.
Raman supports AI infrastructure and regulation together, but her data-center support has softened over 2026 as she added water and grid conditions.
She is the only member in this set to attach a due-process condition to red-flag laws rather than oppose or endorse them outright.
